L01.why: Active 'has preserved' needs a singular agent subject plus an object; the other three cover more subject/voice combinations, but a singular active subject could still license it.

L02.why: 'have' fits only a plural or I/you subject in present tense, the narrowest of the four, but such a subject could exist.

L03.why: Bare plural active 'repeatedly seal' needs a plural agent and an object; plausible enough that it cannot be ruled out.

L04.why: Two colons bracketing an appositive, the second directly before 'and', is never standard punctuation in any sentence.

L05.why: Future perfect 'will have been dismissed' is the rarest fit in a narrative passage, but a forward-looking sentence could require it.

L06.why: 'were still concealed' needs a plural subject in past tense; possible but only one of four subject/tense combinations.

L07.why: No punctuation between 'oxygen' and 'any' likely fuses two units, though a phrase like 'of oxygen any longer' could make it correct.

L08.why: Past perfect 'had kept out' needs an earlier-past frame; possible depending on hidden context.

L09.why: 'has determined' needs a singular agent subject and an object; plausible in some sentences, so not certain.

L10.why: A semicolon before the title requires an independent clause to follow and precede; possible, so not certain.

L11.why: 'has hauled' needs a singular subject in present perfect; one of several viable combinations.

L12.why: 'are now digitizing' needs a plural agent subject with an object; any option could fit some subject.

L13.why: Active past perfect 'had actually brought' needs an agent and object in an earlier-past frame; possible but narrow.

L14.why: No punctuation may fuse an introductory phrase with the main clause, though a sentence like 'at high magnification deep structures appear' is grammatical.

L15.why: The participle 'heading' cannot serve as a main verb, but it could be correct as a modifier, so not certain.

L16.why: 'having left' is a perfect participle that fails as a main verb, but it could be correct as an introductory or trailing modifier.
